MIAMI, Florida (CNN)  -- Prosecutors in Florida are taking a new look at the 2007 death of Anna Nicole Smith to see if recent evidence that California investigators gathered might cause them to open an inquiry. Prosecutors in Florida are reviewing evidence gathered in California for a probe into Anna Nicole Smith's death. Howard K. Stern -- Smith's longtime partner and attorney -- and two doctors were charged this month in California with conspiring to furnish drugs to Smith before her fatal overdose. "Our prosecutors have met with representatives of the Los Angeles County district attorney's office and the California Department of Justice and discussed the evidence they have turned up in their investigation," said Ron Ishoy, a spokesman for Broward County State Attorney Michael Satz. "We are now examining that evidence to see where it might lead in relation to Ms. Smith's death here in Broward County in 2007." The Broward County state attorney's office never opened a probe into Smith's death but assisted the Seminole police in its investigation in the days afterward. Smith, 39, was pronounced dead February 8, 2007, after being discovered unconscious in her hotel room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida. A coroner said she died from an accidental overdose of prescription drugs. Officials said both prescription and over-the-counter drugs were found in Smith's system, including three anti-depressant or anti-anxiety drugs. Human growth hormone and chloral hydrate, a sleep medication, also were found in toxicology tests, officials said. Stern and Drs. Khristine Eroshevich and Sandeep Kapoor were charged in California with several felonies, including conspiring to furnish controlled substances, unlawfully prescribing a controlled substance and obtaining fraudulent prescriptions from June 2004 through January 2007 -- only weeks before Smith's death. Kapoor and Eroshevich also were charged with obtaining a prescription for opiates by "fraud, deceit or misrepresentation." And each was charged with one count of obtaining a prescription for opiates by giving a false name or address, prosecutors said. "Anna was the center of a cruel tabloid feeding frenzy," Eroshevich's attorney, Adam Braun, told CNN in a statement after his client was charged. "In the face of this, Dr. Eroshevich did her best to help the patient while protecting what little privacy Anna had left. Any actions were done with the patient's well-being in mind and were certainly not criminal."  Watch allegations over photos and the doctor » . California Attorney General Jerry Brown said the doctors and Stern devised a plan to use fake names so Smith could be prescribed "thousands of pills." The former Playboy playmate and reality TV star was drugged "almost to the point of stupefaction," Brown said. "The quantity of the drugs, the variety of the drugs, the combination at any given point, and her continuing to use that -- that, to a professional, is clear evidence of addiction," Brown said Friday. "These cocktails of methadone and anti-depressants and sleeping pills and Xanax, you put all that into a cocktail, it explodes and can cause death, injury and permanent morbidity and disability."

MIAMI, Florida (CNN) — Florida prosecutors are reassessing Anna Nicole Smith’s 2007 death to determine whether newly obtained evidence from a California investigation warrants opening a formal inquiry.

Ron Ishoy, spokesman for Broward County State Attorney Michael Satz, said local prosecutors met with officials from the Los Angeles County district attorney’s office and the California Department of Justice to discuss information uncovered during their investigation.

“We are now examining that evidence to see where it might lead in relation to Ms. Smith’s death here in Broward County in 2007,” Ishoy said.

Although the Broward County state attorney’s office did not launch its own investigation into Smith’s death, it helped Seminole police with their inquiry in the days that followed.

Smith, 39, was found unconscious in her room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida, and was declared dead on February 8, 2007. The coroner determined that she died from an accidental overdose of prescription medication.

Officials said toxicology testing detected both prescription and nonprescription substances in her body. These included three medications used to treat depression or anxiety, as well as human growth hormone and the sleep aid chloral hydrate.

Earlier this month, California authorities charged Smith’s longtime companion and lawyer, Howard K. Stern, along with physicians Khristine Eroshevich and Sandeep Kapoor. Prosecutors accused them of conspiring to supply Smith with drugs before the overdose that killed her.

The three defendants face multiple felony counts, including conspiracy to provide controlled substances, illegal prescribing of controlled drugs and securing prescriptions through fraud. Authorities said the alleged conduct occurred between June 2004 and January 2007, ending only weeks before Smith died.

Kapoor and Eroshevich were additionally accused of acquiring an opiate prescription through “fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.” Prosecutors also charged each of them with one count of obtaining an opiate prescription by supplying a false name or address.

After Eroshevich was charged, her attorney, Adam Braun, told CNN in a statement that Smith had been subjected to a vicious frenzy of tabloid attention. He said Eroshevich had tried to care for Smith while preserving the small amount of privacy she still had. According to Braun, everything the doctor did was intended to protect her patient’s welfare and was not criminal.

California Attorney General Jerry Brown alleged that Stern and the two doctors created a scheme involving false names that allowed Smith to receive “thousands of pills.” Brown said the former Playboy model and reality television personality was medicated “almost to the point of stupefaction.”

Speaking Friday, Brown said the number and range of drugs, the combinations in which they were taken and Smith’s continued use of them would constitute obvious evidence of addiction to a medical professional. He warned that mixtures involving methadone, antidepressants, sleeping medications and Xanax can have explosive consequences, potentially resulting in death, injury, lasting illness or disability.

The review does not mean that charges will be filed, but it could lead to the county’s first formal prosecutorial investigation into the circumstances surrounding Smith’s death.

Prosecutors would also have to determine whether the conduct fell within Florida’s jurisdiction and whether sufficient admissible evidence remains to support criminal charges.

Attorneys for Stern and the doctors have maintained that they were trying to help Smith cope with chronic pain, insomnia and emotional distress rather than supply her with drugs for improper purposes. The defendants were expected to contest the California allegations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the charges against Howard K. Stern and doctors Khristine Eroshevich and Sandeep Kapoor for allegedly supplying Anna Nicole Smith with prescription drugs before her fatal overdose.
counterfactuals.output:
## Charges in the Anna Nicole Smith prescription-drug case

California prosecutors charged **Howard K. Stern**, Smith’s lawyer and companion, and physicians **Dr. Khristine Eroshevich** and **Dr. Sandeep Kapoor** in 2009 with conspiring to supply the model with large quantities of controlled prescription drugs before her death.

### Prosecution’s allegations

The case focused on prescriptions issued between 2004 and Smith’s death on **February 8, 2007**. Prosecutors alleged that:

- The defendants obtained or prescribed powerful drugs—including sedatives, anti-anxiety medication, opioids and methadone—without a legitimate medical purpose.
- Prescriptions were issued in excessive quantities or to a person prosecutors characterized as dependent on prescription drugs.
- Several prescriptions were written under aliases, including **“Michelle Chase,”** to conceal that Smith was the intended patient.
- Stern helped arrange and collect drugs, while Eroshevich and Kapoor allegedly violated their professional duties as physicians.

The counts included various combinations of:

- Conspiracy to obtain and furnish controlled substances
- Obtaining prescriptions through fraud, deceit or misrepresentation
- Prescribing controlled substances to an addict
- Prescribing without a legitimate medical purpose
- Using false names in connection with prescriptions

The precise number of counts changed as the case proceeded. At trial, Stern and Eroshevich each faced nine counts, while Kapoor faced six.

### Connection to Smith’s death

The defendants were **not charged with homicide or directly causing Smith’s death**. A Florida medical examiner ruled that she died from an **accidental overdose**, principally involving the sedative chloral hydrate combined with several benzodiazepines and other medications; a severe infection and pneumonia were contributing factors.

Prosecutors nevertheless used evidence about the volume and manner of prescribing to argue that the defendants had facilitated Smith’s drug use.

### Defense position

The defense maintained that:

- Smith suffered from chronic pain, insomnia, anxiety, migraines and seizures, and was devastated by the death of her son Daniel in September 2006.
- The medications were prescribed as legitimate treatment.
- Aliases were commonly used to protect the privacy of celebrities, not to commit fraud.
- Smith was not an “addict” within the meaning of the relevant California prescribing laws.
- Stern was not a doctor and relied on licensed physicians’ medical decisions.

### Trial and verdicts

In October 2010:

- **Kapoor was acquitted of all charges.**
- **Stern was convicted on two conspiracy-related counts** involving the use of false names to obtain prescriptions.
- **Eroshevich was convicted on four counts**, including conspiracy and obtaining prescriptions by fraud or under false names; the jury did not reach verdicts on some additional allegations.

The trial judge later set aside Stern’s felony convictions and substantially reduced Eroshevich’s remaining conviction, reasoning that use of aliases did not necessarily establish criminal intent and that the prosecution had overreached. An appellate court subsequently ordered some convictions reinstated, but after further proceedings the trial court again dismissed the felony case against Stern in the interests of justice. Eroshevich’s remaining offense was treated as a misdemeanor, resulting in probation and a small fine.

### Final practical outcome

- **Sandeep Kapoor:** acquitted.
- **Howard K. Stern:** no surviving criminal conviction from the case.
- **Khristine Eroshevich:** ultimately received misdemeanor-level punishment rather than a felony sentence.

Thus, although the prosecution portrayed the matter as an unlawful prescription-drug conspiracy surrounding a vulnerable celebrity, it did not establish that any of the three defendants criminally caused Smith’s fatal overdose.

counterfactuals.output:
Following California’s March 2009 criminal case, Florida authorities began reviewing evidence gathered there to determine whether Anna Nicole Smith’s February 2007 death warranted further investigation or charges. Florida had previously ruled her death an accidental overdose—primarily chloral hydrate combined with other prescription drugs—and had not found evidence of homicide. The new review did not itself change that finding or establish that anyone caused her death.

California Attorney General Jerry Brown charged Smith’s companion and lawyer, Howard K. Stern, and physicians Sandeep Kapoor and Khristine Eroshevich with conspiring to supply Smith with controlled substances through fraud. Brown alleged that the defendants:

- obtained prescriptions under fictitious or third-party names;
- concealed Smith’s identity and drug use from pharmacists;
- prescribed excessive quantities of sedatives, opiates and other controlled drugs despite knowing she was dependent on them; and
- used the doctors’ licenses to keep an addict supplied with medication.

Brown emphasized that the California prosecution concerned fraudulent prescribing practices, not criminal responsibility for Smith’s death. Florida’s role was to examine the California evidence and decide whether it justified reopening or expanding its own case; at that stage, no new Florida charges had been announced.

counterfactuals.output:
**Broward prosecutors may examine prescribing practices after Anna Nicole Smith overdose ruling**

**FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. —** Broward County prosecutors may open an inquiry into the prescription drugs obtained by Anna Nicole Smith after the county medical examiner concluded that the former Playboy model died from an accidental overdose involving a powerful sedative and several other medications.

Smith, 39, was found unresponsive Feb. 8, 2007, at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida. Broward County Medical Examiner Dr. Joshua Perper later determined that she died from “combined drug intoxication,” with the sleeping medication chloral hydrate identified as the principal cause. Other prescription drugs—including anti-anxiety medications, muscle relaxants and painkillers—were found in her system.

The death was classified as accidental, and investigators said they found no evidence that Smith intended to kill herself or that anyone deliberately poisoned her. That conclusion, however, does not necessarily resolve questions about how she obtained so many medications, whether they were medically justified and whether doctors or others violated Florida prescription-drug laws.

The Broward State Attorney’s Office could review the medical examiner’s findings, police reports, pharmacy records and prescriptions to determine whether a criminal investigation is warranted. Prosecutors would be particularly interested in reports that some prescriptions associated with Smith were written under other names, including the name of her companion and attorney, Howard K. Stern.

Using an alias is not automatically a crime. Celebrities sometimes receive prescriptions under alternate names to protect their privacy, and a physician may prescribe several drugs if there is a legitimate medical need. But prosecutors could investigate whether any prescriptions were written without a proper examination, issued for no valid medical purpose, fraudulently obtained or diverted from the person whose name appeared on the label.

Authorities also could look at whether multiple doctors prescribed overlapping medications without knowing what Smith was already taking. Chloral hydrate can dangerously suppress breathing and the central nervous system, particularly when combined with benzodiazepines and other sedating drugs. The medical examiner said no single one of the additional medications was present at a lethal level, but their combined effect increased the danger.

Smith had also been suffering from a severe infection and flu-like illness in the days before her death. Those conditions may have weakened her, but they did not eliminate possible legal questions surrounding the supply and administration of the medications.

Any prosecutorial inquiry would be separate from the determination of the manner of death. A finding of accidental overdose means the evidence did not support homicide or suicide; it does not bar charges involving improper prescribing, prescription fraud, controlled-substance violations or medical misconduct.

Before deciding whether to proceed, Broward prosecutors would likely seek complete toxicology results, prescription records and interviews with Smith’s doctors, nurses, pharmacists and companions. They would also have to determine which medications were prescribed or dispensed in Florida and which originated in other states, potentially requiring cooperation with outside law-enforcement and medical-licensing authorities.

At this stage, a review would not mean that any doctor, pharmacist or member of Smith’s entourage had committed a crime. Prosecutors would need evidence that someone knowingly acted outside legitimate medical practice or illegally obtained, distributed or administered a controlled substance.

The central question is therefore no longer whether Smith’s death was intentional. It is whether the chain of prescriptions that placed a potentially fatal combination of sedatives in her reach was lawful—and whether anyone should be held criminally responsible for how those drugs were obtained or managed.

**California investigators allege Anna Nicole Smith obtained thousands of pills under false names**

LOS ANGELES — California investigators alleged that Anna Nicole Smith received thousands of prescription pills through prescriptions written under fictitious names, as authorities pursued charges against members of the late model’s inner circle.

Investigators said doctors supplied Smith with powerful medications—including sedatives, painkillers and anti-anxiety drugs—while using aliases or the names of other people to conceal that she was the intended patient. Prosecutors described the prescribing as part of a conspiracy to provide controlled substances to Smith without a legitimate medical purpose.

Smith, 39, died in a Hollywood, Florida, hotel in February 2007. A Florida medical examiner ruled her death an accidental overdose involving the sedative chloral hydrate and several other prescription drugs.

Florida officials said they reviewed the evidence provided by California authorities but found no basis to reopen their criminal investigation into Smith’s death. The Broward County State Attorney’s Office said the California allegations did not alter its conclusion that there was insufficient evidence to bring homicide or other criminal charges in Florida.

The California case focused on whether those close to Smith unlawfully obtained and furnished prescription drugs, rather than on whether anyone intentionally caused her death. The accused denied wrongdoing, and the claims remained allegations pending resolution in court.
